cim: Russia is bringing young foreign influencers to occupied Ukraine, encouraging them to share their highly curated experiences, to legitimize its occupation (Linda Hourani/The Kyiv Independent)
cim_eredeti: Russia is bringing young foreign influencers to occupied Ukraine, encouraging them to share their highly curated experiences, to legitimize its occupation (Linda Hourani/The Kyiv Independent)
szoveg_eredeti:
Invited on an all-expenses-paid trip to occupied Ukraine, young visitors were given a carefully curated view of life under Russian rule — and encouraged to share it with the world.

L, R: Nor Arif Prastyo, a delegate from Indonesia, and (R) Baiel Abdybekov of Kyrgyzstan and Peter Vesko of South Africa hold rifles at a shooting range in Russian-occupied Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, in September 2026. C: Eclat Allan, a participant from Tanzania, holds a Russian flag. (Nor Arif Prastyo / Instagram, Eclat Allan / Instagram, Baiel Abdybekov / Instagram)

On the social media accounts of a group of young foreign visitors touring the Russian-occupied part of Donetsk Oblast, the war-ravaged region is presented as an appealing travel destination.

In Instagram videos, the visitors release white doves — symbols of peace — into the sky and stroll through the Mariupol Drama Theater, rebuilt after Russian forces destroyed it during the 2022 siege. But their next stop is a shooting range, puncturing the fragile illusion of peace they have carefully constructed.

"First time ever holding a gun and the only instruction I got was in Russian, also didn't expect the recoil to hit THIS hard," Indonesian law graduate Nor Arif Prastyo wrote under a photo of himself with a rifle.

Prastyo was one of 15 young people from Africa, Asia, Latin America, and Europe brought to the partially occupied region as guests of the International Festival of Youth, a Russian state-backed event held in mid-September as a revival of a Soviet-era tradition.

The tour of Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast offered visitors a carefully staged portrayal of life under Russian rule. Experts told the Kyiv Independent that the visit was part of a broader effort to whitewash Russia’s international image, legitimize its occupation and turn the visitors into unwitting amplifiers of Russian propaganda.

Russia first seized parts of Donetsk Oblast, including the regional capital of Donetsk, in 2014. Following the launch of its full-scale invasion in 2022, Russian forces occupied additional cities across the region, including Mariupol.

The region remains devastated, and the occupied territories are ranked as the least free places in the world.

But social media posts of the young foreigners Russia took to Donetsk Oblast present the occupied territories as welcoming and thriving. They also ignore Russia's repression and its responsibility for the devastation of cities and the deaths of thousands of civilians.

The Kyiv Independent analyzed social media posts, obtained the program's itinerary, and spoke with a source with direct knowledge of the program to examine what the participants' accounts leave out.

The International Festival of Youth is funded by the Russian state and organized primarily by the Federal Agency for Youth Affairs, a state body also known as Rosmolodezh.

For 2026, the Russian World Youth Festival Directorate, which runs the event, was allocated 4.7 billion rubles ($57 million), nearly five times its funding the year before, independent Russian outlet Agentstvo reported, citing the federal budget.

"Consider it a quid pro quo: they get to travel to Russia for free, but they must only say good things about Russia."

In its promotional materials, the festival says its mission is to help shape "a multipolar world" — a term the Kremlin uses to describe a global order that limits Western dominance and gives Russia a greater role in international affairs.

This year's main event in Yekaterinburg brought together around 10,000 participants, half of them from abroad, according to the organizers.

Much of the festival centered on entertainment, with concerts, folk shows, and a performance featuring more than 1,000 artists. Woven into it was a political message.

Russian President Vladimir Putin addressed the opening ceremony online on Sept. 13, and his speech made its way onto delegates' social media, with footage of them posing with their national flags in front of the screen.

Russia’s approach has remained the same in recent years, said Andrey Makarychev, a professor of regional political studies at the University of Tartu in Estonia.

The Kremlin uses such cultural events to "demonstrate the futility of Western attempts to isolate and sanction Russia, to culturally integrate into the so-called 'global majority' (the global South), and to normalize the ongoing war," he told the Kyiv Independent.

Guests could also visit an exhibition on "Ukrainian neo-Nazism," translated into seven languages, including Arabic, Chinese, and Spanish, Russian state media reported. Displayed at the exhibition was a quote by Putin claiming that Ukrainian statehood is built on neo-Nazi ideology.

The claim has been a staple of Russian propaganda since 2014 and has served as a pretext for the full-scale invasion. The claim has been debunked on multiple occasions, with far-right parties winning less than 2% of the vote in Ukraine's 2019 parliamentary election, and failing to enter parliament.

To be selected for the festival, candidates had to record a video introduction and write an essay. Organizers favored applicants who were active on social media and could create content for their audiences, a source with direct knowledge of the program told the Kyiv Independent, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to safety concerns.

Most participants paid nothing for the trip. According to the festival's promotion materials, organizers covered flights, accommodation, and food. Some participants with partially funded spots had to pay for their flight tickets.

"Consider it a quid pro quo: they get to travel to Russia for free, but they must only say good things about Russia," the source said.

After four days in Yekaterinburg, participants split into smaller groups for regional programs, including in the occupied part of Donetsk Oblast and in Abkhazia, a Russian-occupied region of Georgia.

The delegation that traveled to occupied parts of Donetsk Oblast included participants from Tanzania, Indonesia, South Africa, Uzbekistan, Brazil, Serbia, and India.

"The group was taken to the Mariupol Drama Theater, which Russia rebuilt after its air strike in March 2022 killed civilians sheltering inside. Amnesty International concluded the attack was a war crime."

Baiel Abdybekov, a participant from Kyrgyzstan, told the Kyiv Independent he had not independently chosen a destination and was sent to certain locations by the organizers.

Entering occupied Ukrainian territory through Russia is illegal under Ukrainian law. In 2023, after a group of Chinese bloggers visited occupied Mariupol, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry moved to ban them from entering Ukraine.

Over five days, the youth festival delegation visited Donetsk, the nearby city of Makiivka, and Mariupol. Several participants later posted on Instagram the flag used by Russian proxies and occupation authorities in Donetsk Oblast.

The group was taken to the Mariupol Drama Theater, which Russia rebuilt after its air strike in March 2022 killed civilians sheltering inside. Amnesty International concluded the attack was a war crime.

None of that was featured in the participants' accounts of the visit.

"I strongly recommend visiting this city, which went through the most severe situations and endured," Radmir Hamdamov, a musician from Uzbekistan, was quoted as saying by the Russian-installed culture authorities in occupied Donetsk.

The said "situations" were a nearly three-month Russian siege that killed at least thousands of civilians and left much of Mariupol in ruins.

In Mariupol, the group met Anton Koltsov, head of the Russian occupation authorities in the city, while in occupied Donetsk, they attended a lecture on the region's history at a university run by the occupation authorities.

Members of the group also fired guns at a shooting range and shared drinks and food with men in camouflage wearing military patches.
